title: Dropping In and Carving
bigQuestion: How do you go from standing at the top of a ramp to riding it smoothly, without pushing at all?

story.title: The Longest Minute
story.kicker: A rider waits at the top of a small ramp, then finds the courage to lean forward.
paragraphs: Jordan stands on the flat top of a small quarter pipe at the skatepark. The ramp is only about as tall as his waist. From up here it looks much taller. His coach, Ms. Rivera, stands on the ramp below him, ready to hold out a hand.

His tail sits on the metal edge at the top. His back foot holds the board steady. The front of the board sticks out over the curved wall, front wheels in the air. All he has to do is put his front foot down and lean.

He waits. A minute goes by. Then another. Other skaters roll past on the flat ground. Jordan's legs feel shaky. "It is okay to take your time," Ms. Rivera says. "Fear is your body telling you to pay attention."

She reminds him of the plan. "Front foot on the front bolts. Chest over your front foot. Lean more than feels right. Keep your knees bent." Jordan has practiced each part on a smaller ramp. He knows the steps.

He takes a slow breath. He places his front foot on the bolts and pushes his weight forward. The front wheels slap onto the ramp. The board rolls down the curve, and Jordan rides all the way across the flat ground. He turns around, smiling, and walks back up to try again.
story.think: What helped Jordan finally lean forward and drop in?

lessons.title: Words for Ramps
lessons.mainIdea: A ramp has a flat top called the deck, a metal edge called the coping, a curved wall called the transition, and a flat bottom.
reading: A quarter pipe is a ramp shaped like one side of a U. At the top is a flat platform where you stand. Skaters call it the deck, just like the top of a board. Along its front edge runs a metal pipe or bar. That edge is the *coping*.

Below the coping the wall curves down to the ground. The curved part is the *transition*. Skaters often shorten it to tranny. The curve is what lets a board roll smoothly from going down to going across.

At the bottom is the flat ground, called the flat bottom. A halfpipe is two quarter pipes facing each other, joined by flat bottom. On a halfpipe you can ride back and forth from one wall to the other.

words.d: the metal pipe or edge along the top of a ramp
the curved part of a ramp between the flat ground and the top
two curved ramps facing each other, like a U

look.title: Draw a Ramp
look.text: Draw a flat line for the ground. On the right side, draw a curve that rises like the inside of a bowl. At the top of the curve, draw a small circle for the coping. Behind it, draw a short flat line for the deck where a rider stands.
look.prompt: Label the flat bottom, the transition, the coping and the deck on your drawing.

check.q: What is the coping?
choices: The flat ground at the bottom
The metal edge along the top of a ramp
check.why: The coping is the metal pipe or edge at the top of a ramp.

check.q: What do skaters call the curved part of a ramp?
check.why: The curve between the flat ground and the top is the transition.

check.q: What is a halfpipe?
choices: Two quarter pipes facing each other
check.why: A halfpipe is two quarter pipes facing each other, shaped like a U.

lessons.title: Start Small with a Coach
lessons.mainIdea: Learn ramp skills on a small, low ramp with a coach or grown-up nearby and all your pads on.
reading: Ramps add height, and height adds speed. So the first ramp should be small and low. Many skateparks have a little quarter pipe for beginners. Choose a ramp with a smooth curve and no cracks.

Wear your helmet, wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads. On a ramp, knee pads are extra important. If you fall, you can drop to your knees and slide down the curve. This is called a knee slide. Practice it on the ramp before you try anything else.
Have a coach or a grown-up with you. They can hold your hand for your first tries. Watch which way other skaters are going. Wait your turn so no one rolls into you. Skateparks run on taking turns.

words.d: a safe way to fall on a ramp by dropping onto your knee pads and sliding down
a person who teaches a skill and helps you practice it safely

look.title: Wear the Gear
look.text: Skateboarders should wear a helmet and other protective gear, such as wrist guards, knee pads and elbow pads, every time they ride.
look.cite: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, skateboarding safety advice
look.prompt: Why might knee pads matter even more on a ramp than on flat ground?

check.q: Why should your first ramp be small and low?
choices: Height adds speed, so a low ramp is gentler
check.why: More height means more speed, so a low ramp keeps your speed gentle while you learn.

check.q: What is a knee slide?
choices: Dropping onto your knee pads and sliding down the ramp
Kneeling on your board to push
check.why: A knee slide is a safe ramp fall onto your knee pads.

check.q: Why do skaters wait their turn at a skatepark?
choices: So no one rolls into anyone else
To let the coping cool down
check.why: Taking turns keeps skaters from crashing into each other.

lessons.title: Rolling Up and Back Down
lessons.mainIdea: Rolling a little way up a ramp and back down backward, called fakie, teaches the feel of the curve.
reading: Before dropping in from the top, learn the ramp from the bottom. Roll slowly toward the ramp across the flat bottom. Keep your knees bent and your weight over the middle of the board. Let the board roll a little way up the curve.

Near the top of your roll, the board slows and stops for a moment. Then gravity pulls it back down. Stay in the same stance and roll down backward. Riding backward in your normal stance is called *fakie*. Keep your eyes looking down the ramp.

Each time, roll a little higher. Your body learns how the curve pushes up on the wheels. If you feel the board wobble, bend your knees more. Rolling fakie on a small ramp is a step toward dropping in.

words.d: rolling backward while standing in your normal stance
the pull that brings everything down toward the ground

look.title: Up, Pause, Back
look.text: Picture a rider rolling slowly toward a small ramp. The board climbs the curve and slows. For one moment it stops. Then it rolls back down, tail first, and out across the flat bottom. The rider never moved her feet.
look.prompt: Where on the ramp is the rider going slowest? Where is she going fastest?

check.q: What is fakie?
choices: Rolling backward in your normal stance
check.why: Fakie means rolling backward while keeping your normal stance.

check.q: What pulls the board back down the ramp after it stops?
check.why: Gravity pulls the board back down the curve.

check.q: The board wobbles as you roll up the ramp. What helps?
check.why: Bent knees help you soak up the curve and stay steady.

lessons.title: Setting Up on the Coping
lessons.mainIdea: To set up a drop-in, the tail sits on the coping and the back foot holds it while the front of the board hangs over the ramp.
reading: A *drop-in* is starting a ramp from the top. First, stand on the deck of the ramp, back from the edge. Set the board so the tail rests on top of the coping. The back wheels sit on the deck side of the coping. The front of the board sticks out over the curve.
Next, put your back foot on the tail. Press down to hold the board still. Now the front wheels float in the air over the ramp. Your front foot stays on the deck for now. You are in the *setup*.

Check the ramp below you. Wait until no one is rolling there. Ask your coach to stand on the ramp and hold out a hand. Take a breath. Your back foot keeps the board locked in place until you are ready.

words.d: starting a ramp by rolling down it from the top
the starting position for a drop-in, with the tail on the coping and the back foot holding it

look.title: The Setup Picture
look.text: Picture the top of a small ramp. The tail rests on the coping. The back wheels sit on the flat deck behind it. The rider's back foot presses the tail. The front wheels hang in the air above the curve. The rider's front foot waits on the deck.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on carpet and act out the setup. Which foot holds the board still?

check.q: In the drop-in setup, where is the tail?
check.why: The tail rests on top of the coping, held there by the back foot.

check.q: Which foot holds the board still in the setup?
check.why: The back foot presses the tail to keep the board locked in place.

check.q: What should you check before dropping in?
choices: That no one is rolling on the ramp below
check.why: Waiting until the ramp below is clear keeps everyone safe.

lessons.title: Lean Forward and Commit
lessons.mainIdea: To drop in, put the front foot on the bolts, lean your chest over it, and commit with bent knees.
reading: From the setup, place your front foot on the front bolts. Keep your back foot on the tail. Now comes the key move. Lean forward and push your weight onto your front foot. The front wheels drop onto the ramp.

Lean your chest out over your front foot, toward the bottom of the ramp. It will feel like too much. That is right. Keep both knees bent so you can soak up the curve. Let both feet press the board flat onto the ramp. Look ahead at the flat bottom, not at your feet.

To *commit* means to go all the way once you start. Halfway leaning is what causes falls. Ride down the curve and across the flat bottom. Then stop or roll up the other side. With a coach's hand, the first tries feel much safer.

words.d: to go all the way with a move once you start it
the bolts near the nose, where the front foot goes for a drop-in

look.title: Drop-In, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Tail on the coping, back foot holding it. Step 2: Front foot on the front bolts. Step 3: Lean your chest over your front foot. Step 4: Front wheels drop onto the ramp. Step 5: Knees bent, eyes ahead. Step 6: Ride across the flat bottom.
look.prompt: Which step do you think feels scariest? How could you practice just that step?

check.q: Where does the front foot go for a drop-in?
check.why: The front foot goes on the front bolts before you lean in.

check.q: What does commit mean in a drop-in?
choices: To go all the way once you start
check.why: Committing means going all the way. Leaning only halfway causes falls.

check.q: Where should you look as you drop in?
check.why: Looking ahead helps your body stay over the board.

lessons.title: Why Leaning Back Slips Out
lessons.mainIdea: Leaning back on a drop-in leaves your weight behind the board, so the board slips out ahead of you.
reading: Many new riders lean back on their first drop-in. It feels safer to keep your body away from the slope. But the board does not wait. Gravity pulls it down the ramp right away. If your weight is back, the board rolls out ahead of you.
Then your feet go forward and your body falls back. You land on your back or bottom. This is a very common drop-in fall. It happens because your weight was not over the board.

The fix is to lean forward, with your chest over your front foot. Your body should stay at a right angle to the ramp, like a pole stuck straight into it. Then your weight stays over the wheels and rides down with the board. If you do fall, try to drop to your knees and slide.

words.d: when the board rolls away ahead of your body and you fall
to tilt your body in one direction

look.title: Two Drop-Ins
look.text: Rider one leans back, away from the ramp. The front wheels touch, the board rolls down, and the rider is left behind. Rider two leans chest over the front foot. Her body sticks out from the ramp at a right angle. She and the board roll down together.
look.prompt: Act out both riders on carpet. Where is each rider's weight?

check.q: What usually happens if you lean back on a drop-in?
choices: You go faster and stay on
The board slips out ahead of you
check.why: When your weight is back, gravity pulls the board down the ramp without you.

check.q: How should your body sit on the ramp during a drop-in?
choices: At a right angle to the ramp, chest over the front foot
Standing straight up and down like on flat ground
check.why: Staying at a right angle to the ramp keeps your weight over the wheels.

check.q: What pulls the board down the ramp as soon as the front wheels touch?
check.why: Gravity pulls the board down the slope right away.

lessons.title: When You Feel Scared
lessons.mainIdea: Fear is a normal signal, and breaking a trick into smaller steps helps you get ready.
reading: Most skaters feel scared before their first drop-in. Your heart beats fast. Your legs may shake. This is your body telling you to pay attention. It does not mean you cannot do it.

Break the trick into smaller steps. Practice the setup without dropping in. Practice knee slides on the ramp. Roll fakie higher and higher. Try your first drop-in on the smallest ramp you can find, with a coach holding your hand.
Take slow, deep breaths before you go. Say the steps out loud: front foot, lean, knees bent. It is fine to wait, and it is fine to come back another day. Every skater learns at their own pace.

words.d: a strong feeling that warns you to be careful
one small part of a bigger skill, practiced on its own

look.title: A Ladder of Steps
look.text: Picture a ladder. Bottom rung: stand in the setup on carpet. Next rung: knee slides on a small ramp. Next: roll fakie halfway up. Next: hold the setup at the top of the small ramp. Top rung: drop in with a coach's hand.
look.prompt: Which rung are you on now? What is the next rung for you?

check.q: What does fear before a drop-in mean?
choices: Your body is telling you to pay attention
check.why: Fear is a normal signal to pay attention. It does not mean you cannot do it.

check.q: Which is a good small step toward a drop-in?
choices: Practicing knee slides on a small ramp
check.why: Knee slides are one small step that gets you ready.

check.q: What can you say out loud before you drop in?
check.why: Saying the real steps helps your body remember them.

lessons.title: Toe Side and Heel Side
lessons.mainIdea: Pressing your toes turns the board toward the toe side; pressing your heels turns it toward the heel side.
reading: You can steer a board without lifting any wheels. Press down with your toes, and the deck tilts. The board turns toward your toe side. Press down with your heels, and the board turns toward your *heel side*.

This works because of the trucks. When the deck tilts, the trucks tip and point the wheels in a new direction. Inside each truck are rubber rings called *bushings*. They squish when you lean, then push the board back to level.
Soft wheels grip the ground well in turns. Wheel softness is measured on a scale called durometer A. Lower numbers are softer. Soft wheels are good for cruising and carving on rough ground.

words.d: the side of the board behind your heels
rubber rings inside the trucks that squish when you lean and help you turn
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn

look.title: Soft to Hard Wheels
look.cite: Typical skateboard wheel range, about 78A to 101A; examples
look.prompt: Which wheel is softest? Which would grip best on rough ground?

check.q: You press down with your toes. Which way does the board turn?
check.why: Pressing your toes tilts the deck and turns the board toward the toe side.

check.q: What do bushings do?
choices: They squish when you lean and help the board turn
They hold the grip tape on
They hold the tail on the coping
check.why: Bushings are rubber rings in the trucks that squish as you lean.

check.q: On the durometer A scale, what does a lower number mean?
check.why: Lower durometer A numbers mean softer wheels.

lessons.title: Long, Smooth Carves
lessons.mainIdea: A carve is a long, smooth turn made by leaning on your toes or heels while you roll.
reading: A *carve* is a long, curving turn. It looks like the letter S drawn on the ground. Start on smooth, flat ground with a grown-up nearby. Push to a slow, steady speed. Put your feet over the bolts with your knees bent.

First, look where you want to go. Turn your head and shoulders that way. Then press gently on your toes for a toe side carve. Hold the lean through the whole turn. Next, shift to your heels for a heel side carve. Linking them makes the S.

A common problem is leaning too hard and too fast. The board turns sharply and you may tip. Lean a little at a time instead. Another problem is stiff legs. Keep your knees soft so your body can move with the board.

words.d: a long, smooth turn made by leaning on your toes or heels while you roll
to join two moves one right after the other

look.title: Draw an S
look.text: Picture chalk lines on a playground. A rider rolls slowly, leans on her toes, and the board curves one way. She shifts to her heels, and it curves the other way. Her wheels leave a long, smooth S. Her shoulders turned first each time.
look.prompt: Walk an S shape on the ground. Where would you switch from toes to heels?

check.q: What is a carve?
choices: A long, smooth turn made by leaning
check.why: A carve is a long, smooth turn done by leaning on toes or heels.

check.q: What should you do first when you start a carve?
choices: Look where you want to go
check.why: Looking and turning your shoulders first leads the board into the turn.

check.q: You lean too hard and almost tip. What is the fix?
choices: Lean a little at a time
check.why: Leaning gradually makes a smooth turn instead of a sharp tip.

lessons.title: How to Pump a Ramp
lessons.mainIdea: Pumping means crouching high on the wall and standing up through the curve, which adds speed without pushing.
reading: On a halfpipe you cannot push with your foot. Instead, you *pump*. Pumping means bending and straightening your legs at the right times. Start by rolling back and forth on a small halfpipe, going a little way up each wall.

Near the top of each wall, bend low in a crouch. As you roll down into the curve, push your legs down and stand up tall. Press into the ramp through the bottom of the curve. Then crouch again as you roll up the next wall.

Crouch high, stand in the curve, crouch high again. Each time you do it right, you roll a little higher. If you stand up too early or too late, nothing changes. Watch a skilled rider and notice when their knees bend and straighten.

words.d: to bend and straighten your legs at the right times on a ramp to gain speed
to bend your knees low, close to the board

look.title: Crouch, Stand, Crouch
look.text: Picture a rider on a small halfpipe. High on the left wall, she crouches low. Rolling down into the curve, she presses with her legs and stands tall. Rolling up the right wall, she crouches again. Each trip, her wheels climb a little higher.
look.prompt: Act out pumping in place: crouch, stand, crouch. When do you stand up?

check.q: What does pumping a ramp mean?
choices: Pushing with your foot on the ramp
Bending and straightening your legs at the right times to gain speed
check.why: Pumping is bending and straightening your legs at the right times.

check.q: When should you stand up tall while pumping?
choices: At the top of the wall
As you roll through the curve
check.why: You stand up and press into the ramp through the bottom of the curve.

check.q: When should you crouch while pumping?
choices: Near the top of each wall
In the middle of the flat bottom only
check.why: You crouch low near the top of each wall, then stand in the curve.

lessons.title: Why Pumping Adds Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Friction takes away a little energy on every trip, and pumping puts energy back from your muscles.
reading: When you roll up a ramp, you slow down. Your motion energy turns into stored energy, because you are higher. When you roll back down, the stored energy turns back into motion energy. On a halfpipe, the two keep trading back and forth.

If that were all, you would roll back and forth forever. But *friction* takes a little energy away on every trip. The wheels rub the ramp, and the bearings rub inside. Some energy becomes heat and sound. So without pumping, each trip goes a little lower.

Pumping puts energy back. When you stand up in the curve, your legs push hard against the ramp. That push comes from your muscles. It adds a little energy each time. Add more than friction takes, and you roll higher and faster.

words.d: a force that slows things down when two surfaces rub together
energy that something has because it is high up; also called potential energy
energy that something has because it is moving; also called kinetic energy

look.cite: Example numbers to show the idea, not measured
look.prompt: In this example, how much lower is each trip? What could the rider do to stop losing height?

check.q: As you roll up a ramp, what does your motion energy turn into?
check.why: Going higher turns motion energy into stored energy.

check.q: Without pumping, why does each trip go a little lower?
choices: Friction takes a little energy away each trip
check.why: Friction turns some energy into heat and sound on every trip.

check.q: Where does the extra energy from pumping come from?
choices: Your muscles pushing against the ramp
check.why: When you stand up in the curve, your leg muscles push and add energy.

review.q: What is the metal edge at the top of a ramp called?
review.why: The coping is the metal edge along the top of a ramp.

review.q: In the drop-in setup, what does the back foot do?
choices: Holds the tail down on the coping
review.why: The back foot presses the tail to hold the board still on the coping.

review.q: Jordan waited a long time before dropping in. What did his coach say fear means?
choices: His body was telling him to pay attention
He was doing the trick wrong
review.why: Fear is a normal signal to pay attention.

review.q: What often causes a fall on a drop-in?
review.why: Leaning back leaves your weight behind and the board slips out.

review.q: What is the right order for a drop-in?
choices: Lean back, front foot on, stand tall
Tail on coping, front foot on bolts, lean forward, ride
Front foot on coping, jump, land
review.why: Set the tail on the coping, put the front foot on the bolts, lean forward and ride down.

review.q: To carve toward your heel side, what do you press?
review.why: Pressing your heels turns the board toward the heel side.

review.q: What does pumping let you do on a halfpipe?
choices: Gain speed without pushing with your foot
review.why: Pumping adds energy from your legs, so you gain speed without pushing.

review.q: What is a safe way to fall on a ramp?
choices: Drop to your knee pads and slide down
review.why: A knee slide lets you slide safely down the ramp on your pads.
